title: The ghats
hookLine: Hindus hold that dying in Kashi, Varanasi, brings liberation, and the cremation fires there never go out

lines: WHY COME HERE AT THE END?
cards: Stone steps run down into a wide river. At one end, people are bathing and praying in the water. A little further along, smoke rises from fires burning right on the steps.
This is Varanasi, the city Hindus also call Kashi, on the Ganges. The steps are called ghats, and at some of them the dead are cremated in the open air. Tradition says those fires never go out.
Why do people come to this city at the end of their lives?

teach.b: First, the steps. A ghat is a flight of steps leading down to the water. Along the river at Varanasi, ghat follows ghat.
People come to bathe, to pray, to float small lamps at dusk. A few of the ghats are for the dead; one is called Manikarnika. Second, the hope.

teach.h: DIE IN KASHI, BE SET FREE.
teach.b: Hindu tradition holds that to die in Kashi brings moksha, liberation from the cycle of birth and death.
Texts that praise the city tell why: tradition says Shiva himself comes to the dying here and speaks a saving word into their ear, carrying them across.
So some people come to Varanasi when they are old or ill, hoping to spend their last days in the city. Third, the fire. Cremation is the usual Hindu custom, though not the only one.
At the burning ghats, the body, wrapped in cloth, is carried down through the lanes, dipped in the river, and laid on a pyre. A close relative lights it. Afterward the ashes are given to the Ganges.
Tradition says the fires at Manikarnika have never been allowed to go out. Fourth, what this place does.
Death is often kept behind a closed door.

Here it happens on the steps, by the water, beside bathers, boats and children. The tradition treats this not as a place of despair but as a place of release, kept in plain sight, in the middle of ordinary life.

how: Hindu families cremate their dead, and some bring them to the burning ghats at Varanasi, where a relative lights the pyre and the ashes are given to the Ganges; some people come to the city in old age hoping to die there.

o: the holy river into which Hindu families give the ashes
riverside temples where the dead lie in state before burial
stone steps down to the river, for bathing, prayer and cremation

games.q: the city on the river — tap the pairs.
p: steps leading down to the water
a burning ghat (tradition: fires never die)

s: at Varanasi, cremations are hidden away from daily life
they happen in the open, on the steps, beside bathers and boats.
Hindu tradition holds that dying in Kashi brings liberation
tradition says Shiva speaks a saving word into the ear of the dying there.
a ghat is a kind of temple
it's a flight of steps leading down to the water.

games.q: you're walking the steps at Varanasi at dusk. smoke rises from fires on the steps, not far from people bathing. what are you seeing?
o: cremations, done in the open by the river.
games.why: the burning ghats. families carry their dead down to the river, and a relative lights the pyre, in plain sight of the city.

practice: If you have a candle and a safe place for it, light it; if not, let any small light nearby be your flame, like the little lamps people set on the river at Varanasi at dusk. Watch how it moves and stays at once.
If someone you've lost comes to mind, let them be there with the light.

wordCard.voice: The ghats: the stone steps down to the river at Varanasi, where Hindus bathe, pray, and cremate their dead, hoping for liberation. Today's word.

orig.note: Hindi: ghat, a flight of steps leading down to a river.

carryVoice: Your line: kept in plain sight. Steps, water, a small flame. That's day seven hundred seventy-two.

sources.ref: Skanda Purana, Kashi Khanda (the praise of Kashi and liberation there)
